chunks: "Inside a hobby servo you have a small DC motor, a gear train, a potentiometer attached to the output shaft and a control chip with an H-bridge.
Every 20 milliseconds I send it a pulse, and the width of that pulse, around 1 to 2 milliseconds, is the target angle.
The chip measures the pulse width and turns it into a target voltage or number.
At the same time it reads the potentiometer, which gives a voltage proportional to the actual shaft angle. The control chip subtracts the two to get an error.

If the error is positive it turns the H-bridge on in one direction, if negative the other direction, and the drive is roughly proportional to the size of the error, so it moves fast when it's far and slows down as it arrives.
When the error falls inside a small deadband, it stops driving.

The gearbox is there because small motors spin fast with little torque; the gears trade speed for torque, and they also put the potentiometer on the slow output side, which gives the angle sensor good resolution.
If you push on the shaft, the pot reading changes, an error appears and the servo pushes back, which is why it holds position."
